title: Power vs. Endurance: The Dual Frontiers of Doping Incentives
text:
Two Opposite Physiological Demands
Athletic disciplines place starkly divergent mechanical constraints on the human body. As visualized above across more than 10,000 Olympic competitors between 1960 and 2016, weightlifters and cyclists occupy radically different physiological profiles. Weightlifters cluster heavily toward elevated body mass relative to height, prioritizing absolute cross-sectional muscle area to generate maximal ground-reaction force. In contrast, road and track cyclists cluster tightly within a narrow, lean corridor where extra upper-body mass represents dead weight that increases rolling resistance and aerodynamic drag.
These divergent biomechanical demands directly dictate the pharmacological incentives observed in anti-doping testing. In sports governed by raw power and short bursts of explosive torque—such as weightlifting, sprinting, and throwing—adverse analytical findings (AAFs) reported by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) have historically been dominated by anabolic androgenic steroids (AAS) and human growth hormone (hGH). These substances directly stimulate muscle protein synthesis and accelerate musculoskeletal recovery from heavy resistance strain.
Conversely, in aerobic endurance disciplines like cycling, distance running, and cross-country skiing, performance is capped by VO2 max, cardiac output, and oxygen delivery to slow-twitch muscle fibers. Consequently, performance enhancement in endurance disciplines centers on blood manipulation—including recombinant human erythropoietin (EPO), blood transfusions, and synthetic oxygen carriers. The distinct clustering in the data explains why anti-doping surveillance cannot apply a one-size-fits-all model: the physiological bottleneck of each sport determines the exact substances athletes are incentivized to pursue.

title: Performance Enhancement in Sports: Anti-Doping Testing Trends
text:
Project Overview
Performance enhancement in competitive athletics represents a complex intersection of physiology, pharmacology, and regulatory oversight. Using testing reports from organizations such as the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency (USADA), this project analyzes how sample volumes, testing protocols, and adverse analytical findings differ across sports and how these dynamics have evolved over recent decades.
Understanding anti-doping data requires understanding the athletes themselves: what physical traits and mechanical demands define each discipline, and what incentives might drive athletes toward specific classes of prohibited substances?

title: Performance Enhancement in Sports: Anti-Doping Testing Trends
text:
Key Analytical Variables
To evaluate testing regimes and detection rates, our analysis focuses on five primary dimensions:








Variable
Description
Analytical Purpose




sport
Athletic discipline (e.g., athletics, cycling, weightlifting, aquatics)
Compares baseline physiology, testing volume, and positivity rates across sports


year
Testing and competition year
Identifies multi-year trends, policy shifts, and improvements in detection sensitivity


test_type
In-competition vs. out-of-competition testing
Evaluates detection timing and unannounced surveillance effectiveness


sample_type
Biological matrix collected (urine vs. blood)
Accounts for differences in detection windows across substance classes


adverse_finding
Binary indicator of an adverse analytical finding (AAF)
Quantifies raw violation counts and calculated positivity percentages

Key Takeaways & Anti-Doping Implications

Biomechanical Specialization: Each sport clusters in a distinct region of physical trait space. Gymnastics demands a compact center of gravity, while basketball and volleyball select for extreme stature.
Dispersion Reflects Sub-disciplines: Athletics exhibits the largest scatter because track and field spans contrasting physiological extremes—from distance runners requiring low mass to throwers relying on maximum inertia.
Incentive Alignment for Performance Enhancement:

Disciplines requiring raw power and explosive leverage (e.g., weightlifting and sprinting) historically present higher risks for anabolic agents.
Aerobic-demanding endurance sports (e.g., cycling, rowing, distance running) present risks centered on oxygen-transport enhancement, such as erythropoietin (EPO) and blood manipulation.

title: How Olympic Swimmers Have Changed
text: The graphic displays 3,707 Olympic swimming athlete-event records across six individual events, with points colored by decade from the early 1900s through 2016. Across 120 years of competition, athlete bodies shifted distinctly upward in height and weight as training modernized and event specialization intensified.
